Court of Queen’s Bench of Alberta

Citation: SJB v
RDBB, 2019 ABQB 624

Date:
20190812

Docket:
4801 169252

Registry:
Calgary

Between:

SJB

Plaintiff

- and -

RDBB

Defendant

Corrected judgment:
A corrigendum was issued on August 13,

_______________________________________________________

Reasons for Judgment

of the

Honourable
Mr. Justice

D.A. Labrenz

_______________________________________________________

Introduction

[
1
]

Mr. RDBB ["Mr. B"] and Ms. SJB ["Ms.
B"] began living together in 1995, married in 2000, and separated in 2014.
They are the parents of two children, a daughter and a son, currently ages 14
and 11. At trial, they asked this Court to decide all issues related to the
breakdown of their marriage, including the division of matrimonial property,
spousal support, child support and parenting. After the hearing, they advised
they would refer the parenting issues to an arbitrator. Ultimately, the
arbitration did not occur as Mr. B. did not provide the necessary funding for
his portion of the proposed arbitration. Mr. B. advised the Court that he was
currently impecunious. Regardless, the parenting issues are again before this
Court.

[
2
]

Mr. B is a 50% shareholder in several corporate
entities that principally own and manage real estate properties in Calgary.
These corporate entities form a substantial part of the matrimonial property.
The parties own two residential properties in Calgary, and have recently sold a
home in Arizona. The parties have a number of debts, including alleged loans
from their respective mothers, each loan said to be evidenced by
contemporaneous documentation. At trial, the Court also heard evidence about
Ms. B's additional indebtedness to her mother arising from post-separation
expenditures.

[
3
]

Mr. B's corporate interests provided him with a
substantial income throughout both the marriage and separation, which Mr. B
received in the form of dividends and extensive shareholder loans. Mr. B earned
this income by taking care of the day-to-day repairs and maintenance of the
corporate properties, collecting rents, etc., while his business partner, Mr.
S, managed the financial side of the business. Ms. B presented expert evidence
about the value of these corporate entities and Mr. B's Guideline income; Mr. B
did not present contradictory expert evidence. Ms. B works as a commercial real
estate broker and the same expert presented evidence as to her Guideline
income.

[
4
]

Since the separation, the children have been
living primarily with Ms. B in the matrimonial home. Mr. B has not been paying
child support at levels commensurate with his income, nor in accordance with
orders of this Court. Ms. B seeks section 3 child support from the date of
separation based on Mr. B's Guideline income, as set out by her expert. Mr. B's
work with the corporate entities has ended and he indicates that he is
currently unemployed. Ms. B seeks ongoing child support based on an imputed
income for Mr. B.

[
5
]

The parties disagree on the reasonableness and
necessity of some of the children's section 7 expenses. The daughter is heavily
involved in dance, while the son plays hockey. Mr. B disagrees with many of the
costs associated with the daughter's dance. By contrast, he is supportive and
actively involved in his son's hockey. Mr. B also disagrees with the son's
attendance at private school and asks that he not be required to contribute
towards its cost. He takes the position that the parties can no longer afford
it and historically, Ms. B's parents helped pay for it.

[
6
]

Finally, Ms. B seeks spousal support on
compensatory and non-compensatory grounds.

[
7
]

The issues to be resolved are as follows:

1.

Parenting

a)

Should
the current parenting schedule remain in place?

b)

Should
Ms. B be granted sole decision-making power?

2.

Matrimonial
property

a)

What
is the value of Mr. B's corporate interests?

b)

Has
each party established the validity of the loans from their respective mothers?

c)

What
is the value of all the other matrimonial property?

d)

How should
the matrimonial property be distributed?

3.

Child
Support

a)

What
is Mr. B's Guideline income?

b)

What
were Mr. B's child support obligations since separation and what are they going
forward?

c)

What
is Ms. B's Guideline income?

d)

What were
the section 7 expenses since separation and how should they be shared in the
past and going forward?

4.

Spousal
support

a)

Is
Ms. B entitled to spousal support?

b)

If
so, what is the proper amount of spousal support and for what
duration?

Mr. B's credibility

[
8
]

As in many, if not most family law trials, there
was some irreconcilable conflict between the testimony of Mr. B and Ms. B. Mr.
B testified that he disclosed everything to the best of his ability and in a
timely manner, but the evidence shows that Ms. B's counsel had difficulty
obtaining proper financial disclosure from Mr. B, and Ms. B's counsel had to
apply to the Court to compel proper financial disclosure. Nor was Mr. B. always
completely cooperative in relation to other litigation steps. For example, Ms.
B had to enlist the help of the Court to compel Mr. B to attend questioning
after he failed to appear on a scheduled questioning date, and furthermore Ms.
B had to enlist the help of the Court to compel Mr. B's proper response to his
undertakings made in response to his questioning.

[
9
]

The cross-examination of Mr. B at trial clearly demonstrated
that Mr. B has been less than forthright with this Court. Mr. B was evasive in
his testimony to the point of refusing to concede clear facts. For example, the
following exchange between Ms. B's counsel and Mr. B in cross-examination is
illustrative. Ms. B's counsel asked Mr. B to explain the discrepancy between his
anticipated income of $110,000 as set out in Mr. B's Statement of Income,
Assets and Liabilities sworn on May 31, 2016 ["May 2016 Statement"],
as compared to the $150,000 that had already been deposited into his bank
account in the first three months of the year:

Q Okay. And if we go to the first page at --
just above "Assets," it says: (as read)

I expect my line 150 income to be $110,000.
And that's at -- in your 2016 stat dec; do you see that?

A I do.

Q Okay. You swore this in May, and I’ve just
shown you evidence that showed you had already taken by March of 2016, $150,000
by way either income or shareholder loan.

A Correct.

Q So why did you inaccurately describe --

A I didn’t.

Q -- your income on this?

A I -- this clearly states I expected.
Obviously, I had more bills come in through lawyers, accountants, and everyone
else that I needed to pull more from my shareholder's loan. So I expected it to
be that, but unfortunately it wasn’t.

Q Okay, but it was already higher.

A Yeah, exactly. It's been more. I expected
it to be that $110,000 –

...

Q And your statutory declaration, which is
sworn in May, says you’re going to earn an income of $110,000. I’m going to
suggest to you by the time you swore this, you had already earned $150,000, and
this is false.

A I -- but again, that would have been
figured out at the end of the year, not at that point in time. I don’t keep
track of a running total what I’ve pulled from the company until I get at the
end of the year.

Q So you didn’t go through and determine --

A No.

Q -- what you thought your income was going
to be?

A No. I expected it to be that, pretty
standard.

[
10
]

Mr. B filed three separate Statements of Income,
Assets and Liabilities, sworn in May 2016, August 2018 ["August 2018
Statement"] and November 2018, respectively. None are comprehensive. For
example, in August 2018, Mr. B failed to disclose the Pump Hill home as an
asset even though he included the mortgage as a liability. Similarly, he
identified a debt for a BMW motor vehicle, but with no corresponding asset. The
May 2016 Statement identified a number of bank accounts that are not included
in the later statements. Meanwhile, the values for his corporate interests
varied from unknown, to $4 million, to $2,251,262.

[
11
]

Mr. B was cross-examined quite extensively at
trial about hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of draws he received into
his bank account from his corporate interests. Mr. B did not provide cogent
evidence about the nature of those draws, the rationale for having received the
monetary draws, or most importantly, to explain why greater amounts of the
money received by Mr. B were not diverted to pay down a growing debt related to
his child and spousal support obligations.

[
12
]

While the value of assets and debts can
fluctuate over time, Mr. B's testimony does not inspire confidence in the veracity
or accuracy of his sworn evidence. Ms. B's counsel showed Mr. B the May 2016
Statement and asked him if he had told the truth in this document. Mr. B said, "I'm
sure. That's my ... best ability, you bet." Mr. B could not confirm that
he had read the oath, or perhaps even the contents of the document itself:

Q Okay. And you would read that before you
signed this?

A Not likely, but --

Q You wouldn’t have read that?

A Not -- not -- that's not my style, no, but
--

Q Well, what --

A -- I would’ve signed it.

Q -- what is your style?

A Just to sign it and move on, but that's
okay. Carry on.

Q No, just hold on. So just to sign --

A Yeah.

Q -- court documents without reading them?

A Yeah, something of that nature. I did not
sign them. I would probably have not read it, no. I just said that twice now.

[
13
]

Ms. B's counsel directed Mr. B to the August
2018 Statement. Again, Mr. B testified that he hadn’t necessarily read the
contents of that document:

Q Okay. And again, this one has the same
oath that everything in here is true.

A Okay.

Q And you understood it to be true?

A If I had read it at the time, I’m sure,
yes.

Q Okay. Did -- can you confirm that you did
read it before you signed it?

A I can’t confirm that, no.

Q You can’t confirm that you read it?

A No. I just said now the second time.

Q Okay. So, is -- is it you evidence that
you signed a statutory declaration without reading it?

A Without possibly reading it, yes.

[
14
]

Likewise, when Ms. B's counsel showed Mr. B an
affidavit he had sworn on May 9, 2016 and asked if he would have told the truth
in this document, Mr. B's response was "I would hope so." As
mentioned, throughout his testimony, Mr. B was unable to explain the
substantial amounts of money coming into or out of his bank accounts. At one
point, he suggested some of the deposits might have been in the nature of
investment income, yet Mr. B's income tax returns for the relevant periods do
not disclose any investment or interest income.

[
15
]

Overall, Mr. B's evidence lacked both
reliability and credibility, most particularly when it came to financial
matters. Where his evidence differs from that of Ms. B or other witnesses, I
prefer the evidence of the other witnesses.

Ms. M's testimony

[
16
]

Ms. B presented Ms. M as a witness. Ms. M was
involved in a relationship with Mr. B after his separation from Ms. B. She and
her children lived with Mr. B and his children for some time. Mr. B strongly
objected to her evidence, arguing she had colluded with Ms. B in preparing her
testimony and that she was driven by anger and vindictiveness. I am troubled by
some aspects of Ms. M's involvement in this case. While some of her testimony
corroborated Ms. B's evidence and contradicted Mr. B's evidence, I have not
relied upon it.

With prejudice settlement offer

[
17
]

In his evidence and argument, Mr. B and his
legal counsel frequently referred to Mr. B's "With Prejudice" full
and comprehensive settlement offer, dated July 9, 2018 (open for acceptance until
July 16, 2018).

[
18
]

Mr. B proposed, for the purposes of settling
the matrimonial property dispute, that he would sell, with the agreement of his
business partner, two apartment buildings owned by one of the corporate
entities to fund a settlement. The settlement offer included terms regarding
parenting, travel with the children, child support and a complete waiver of
spousal support. Mr. B testified that Ms. B's counsel rejected the offer
without explanation. He went so far as to imply that the full responsibility
for the trial lay at Ms. B's feet, if only she had accepted his offer, they
could have avoided the time and expense of a trial.

[
19
]

I disagree with this submission. The offer was
merely that - an offer. Ms. B was entitled to reject the offer on the basis
that she did not find it to be satisfactory. I accept the explanation provided
by Ms. B's counsel that the settlement offer was not premised upon the sale of
all of Mr. B's corporate interests (Mr. S, the business partner, did not agree
at the time to sell the interests of one of the entities, which I shall call "BI
Corp."), the offer did not compensate Ms. B for a debt she had incurred
with her mother, and the offer contemplated a complete waiver of spousal support.

[
20
]

In short, I have not found the With Prejudice Settlement
Offer to have been useful in making any of the determinations that I am called
upon to make at trial.

1. Parenting

a) Should the current parenting schedule remain in place?

[
21
]

The parties attempted to resolve the issues
arising from the breakdown of their marriage outside of court. Ms. B explained
that the parties appeared twice before a Dispute Resolution Officer, attended
four or five mediation sessions, and ultimately attempted mediation/arbitration.
These attempts at extra-judicial resolution were ultimately unsuccessful as Mr.
B engaged in a pattern of discharging his legal counsel, or at other times he refused
to continue paying for his portion of the costs associated with the resolution
processes.

[
22
]

I find that Mr. B was not genuinely interested
in following through with these largely cooperative resolution methods. While
it is true that Mr. B made a with prejudice settlement offer, the offer itself
was one-sided, in the sense that it was not negotiated; instead, the offer made
by Mr. B represented his considered view of a fair resolution in the
circumstances. At that point, Ms. B had two diametrically opposed options:
accept the offer, or refuse the offer and proceed to trial.

[
23
]

In my view, the failed resolution processes
attempted by the parties is emblematic of the inability of Mr. B and Ms. B to
work cooperatively through their differences towards settlement or resolution. This
is important because it gives me little confidence that Mr. B and Ms. B will be
able to work together cooperatively to successfully resolve any issues relating
to the children. The history of this protracted litigation, which involved case
management and many court applications, confirms my conclusion that any expectation
of cooperation between the parties would be ill-founded.

[
24
]

At the time of the trial, the daughter of the
marriage ["AB"] was 14 years of age. Ms. B described her as a "kind,
sweet girl" who suffers from anxiety and loneliness. AB has ADHD, and a
painful adolescent back condition that affects her spine called Schermann's
disease. Ms. B indicates that AB's love for dancing has provided her with some
relief from her medical condition; however, Mr. B was not generally supportive
of AB's dancing, largely for financial reasons.

[
25
]

The parties’ son ["JB"], who was 11 at
the time of the trial, also has issues with ADHD, but Ms. B explained that JB receives
beneficial attention in private school. This is confirmed by independent
reports placed into evidence. By agreement, the Court received a report from a
psychologist who advised that JB had been diagnosed with a mild specific
learning disorder with impairment in mathematics.

[
26
]

I find that Ms. B is particularly attenuated to
her son's circumstances, and I have confidence that Ms. B will always act in JB's
best interests. Mr. B, while greatly involved in his son's athletic interests
in playing ice hockey, did not seem to be particularly sensitive to either of
his son or his daughter's medical or learning impairments. This may be
explained, in part, because during the marriage Ms. B performed the role of
being the primary care-giver to her children, and it was obvious to the Court
that the children are primarily bonded to and reliant on their mother.

[
27
]

The relationship the children have had with
their father post-separation was the subject of an independent report. In 2016,
a therapist began seeing the children as their advocate or voice, with the
additional responsibility of helping the children adjust to the separation. The
Court received a report written by this therapist by consent, and more
particularly without any objection or opposition to its hearsay nature.
Undoubtedly, neither party had any desire to have their children attend before
the Court to give evidence in the proceedings.

[
28
]

Both children reported to the therapist that they
were happy with their mother, and that they received more attention when they
were with her. When with their father, by contrast, they reported "fighting"
because of Mr. B's inability to get them to school on time, and the limited
access to their mother by phone. The children both felt that while Mr. B was
present, he was not attentive to them. In particular, the children complained
that Mr. B did not spend time with them, and instead that he was always on the
phone with his partner, or on his computer.

[
29
]

Ms. B provided some confirming evidence of the
loneliness the children felt during Mr. B's parenting time, and told the Court
that when the children were with Mr. B, she would often receive phone calls
from them, crying and asking to be picked up. My clear impression is that the children
often felt neglected when in their father's company, and that they were never
made to feel that they were his priority. Sadly, JB told the therapist that he
believed his father did not love him, and reported that his father made
comments about Ms. B to the effect of wishing she was dead. Ms. B recalled such
a comment made by Mr. B in the presence of her and the children. On that occasion,
Mr. B said that he wished Ms. B were buried six feet under.

[
30
]

Ms. B also advised the Court that Mr. B
frequently involved the children in talking about adult issues relating to the
separation and pending divorce; for example, Ms. B came to learn from her then
8-year-old son that Mr. B had re-partnered. The therapist reported that JB did
not want to spend time with his father and AB did not feel welcome in his home.
To provide some context and understanding, Mr. B could, at times be mentally
cruel to his children. For example, the children, who are Jewish, reported to
the therapist that Mr. B made an anti-Semitic remark to AB and placed a picture
of Jesus outside her bedroom door. On other occasions, Mr. B would say to the
children that he hated Jews. While Mr. B, who himself was raised Jewish,
initially denied telling AB that he hated Jews, later in his cross-examination,
he tellingly said that he did not believe he would make such a statement. Still
later in cross-examination, Mr. B said he did not believe he would make this
statement as a non-practising "fellow Jew."

[
31
]

I have no doubt the statements were made and
that the statements were very hurtful and confusing to the children. Mr. B's
motivations in making these statements are not so easy to understand. The
statements call into question both Mr. B's maturity and judgment. I am not
convinced that Mr. B has at all times the ability to make proper decisions in his
children's best interests.

[
32
]

The current custody arrangement does not provide
extensive parenting time to Mr. B, essentially every second weekend, along with
Thursday evenings. Despite the relatively limited duration of Mr. B's parenting
time with the children, Ms. B advised the Court that the children often returned
to her without having completed their homework. In addition, as I have earlier
mentioned, Mr. B has found it difficult to get the children to school in a
timely fashion.

[
33
]

Notwithstanding the obvious acrimony between the
parties, the inability to properly communicate, and Mr. B's disparaging remarks
(bordering on threats) towards Ms. B, Ms. B made it abundantly clear that she hopes
her children will develop a positive relationship with their father. This is to
Ms. B's credit, and I accept Ms. B's evidence that she will do whatever she can
to foster this relationship. Ms. B described the time the children spent being
parented as being the children's time; meaning that the time spent with each
parent did not belong to either parent, but to the children themselves. I find
that Ms. B's attitude towards the children is positive, encouraging and
nurturing.

[
34
]

Mr. B does not oppose the parenting status quo that
was worked out between the parties in mediation, and I agree that the parenting
schedule which has been in place since the time of separation is appropriate in
the circumstances, to the extent that Mr. B refrains from making further
harmful comments in front of the children. It is my view, however, that given
the age of the children, and with a view to the children's best interests, the
Court should not make an order that would compel them to spend time with Mr. B if
either child decides not to do so. I am comforted in coming to this conclusion based
on my finding that Ms. B has never made any attempt to alienate the children
from their father, and has instead encouraged the children's ongoing contact
with Mr. B.

[
35
]

I, too, encourage such ongoing contact between
the children and their father, yet I recognize that given their experiences
with their father post-separation, the children need to be given a voice. They
are both at an age where if not now, then very soon, they will vote with their
feet if the more negative paternal behaviours I have described continue. The
children are of an age that the custody order, practically speaking, requires
their cooperation and, in turn, a careful consideration of their views and
preferences. Additionally, as mentioned, Mr. B has not always acted in the best
interests of his children. It is the Court's finding that in some situations Mr.
B has acted in a manner that is injurious to his children's mental health,
which is quite obviously contrary to their best interests.

[
36
]

With these qualifications, I accept that the
status quo as to the parenting schedule is in the best interests of the
children. In doing so, I recognize the objective of maximizing contact with
both parents to the extent such contact is consistent with the children's best
interests:
Divorce Act
, s 16(10)
.
While it is desirable to
maximize contact with both parents as has been recognized by the Supreme Court
of Canada in
Young v Young,
1993 CanLII 34 (SCC)
, [1993] 4 SCR 3, both that decision
and
section 16(10)
of the
Divorce Act
make it clear that the court must
only order such contact as is consistent with the children's best interests. As
McLachlin J., as she then was succinctly stated, "This means that parental
preferences and ‘rights’ play no role":
Young

at para
117
.

[
37
]

With these considerations in mind, the Court
agrees with Ms. B's proposal as to the timing and manner of the exchanges of
the children as between the parties. Finally, the Court agrees that the
children should spend each Jewish holiday with Ms. B, equally share the
children during summer and winter breaks from school, and alternate spring
breaks as between the parties.

b) Should Ms. B be granted sole decision-making power?

[
38
]

I have little confidence that Mr. B will
cooperate with Ms. B in making major or minor decisions regarding the children's
best interests, nor am I confident that Mr. B will always put his children's
best interests ahead of his own.

[
39
]

As one example, simple matters such as obtaining
from Mr. B his consent for the children to travel has resulted in unwarranted difficulties
for Ms. B. In the past, Mr. B would never commit in a timely manner to the
dates Ms. B proposed for travel out of the country with the children. Ms. B
told the court about instances where she ended up paying inflated airline
prices because Mr. B's consent to travel was delayed, and Ms. B encountered situations
where she was reduced to begging Mr. B for his consent. This type of difficulty
continued even after the trial evidence was concluded.

[
40
]

Mr. B explained that he did not grant permission
to the children to travel over the last winter break because of a disputed
Enmax utility bill that he felt Ms. B should have paid. In doing so, it is
clear that Mr. B is quite prepared to place his perceived interests in a place
of paramountcy to those of his children's best interests in travelling. In
particular, to be clear, Mr. B expressed no genuine concern or objection to the
travel itself. Instead he sought to leverage his children's travel interests
against his interests in having Ms. B pay the unpaid Enmax bill.

[
41
]

The parties’ acrimonious inability to
cooperatively resolve any disputes regarding the children is not confined to
travel, but extends into other areas of critical importance such as education
and health. For example, citing financial reasons, Mr. B did not agree on JB's
continued attendance at private school. While the financial concerns are
understandable, the Court remains concerned that there is no present mechanism
to settle the frequent and ongoing disputes between the parties. Further, and
more importantly, the Court has no reasonable expectation that the level of cooperation
will improve soon, if at all. Certainly, the trial process itself cannot be
expected to promote a sense of willing cooperation.

[
42
]

In my view, it is not in the best interests of
the children to place them in a situation where they will be exposed to the
continued and repeated acrimony between their parents, which will at a minimum,
require ongoing court applications as a form of constant dispute resolution:
Rensonnet
v Uttl,
2016 ABCA 196
. As Fraser CJA pointedly stated in
Richter
v Richter,
2005 ABCA 165
at para
11
: "...joint custody and shared
parenting arrangements ought not to be ordered where the parents are in
substantial conflict with each other, and certainly not before trial especially
when there is significant disagreement on the evidence. The best interests of a
child are not well served by imposing regimes which invite continued court
applications on all matters, big and small." I find these comments made by
the Chief Justice are equally applicable here.

[
43
]

Largely because of the continued and ongoing
parental conflict, and equally because I find Mr. B is not always willing to
act in his children's best interests, I am satisfied that it is in the best
interests of the children to grant Ms. B sole decision-making power. The
parties will share ongoing guardianship of the children, with Ms. B having the
final or ultimate decision-making authority. Ms. B may travel with the children
without Mr. B's consent. Mr. B will be entitled to obtain information about the
children's health or education directly from the service providers, and the
mother will facilitate his ability to do so by advising doctors, dentists,
school teachers and administrators of this requirement. Ms. B will provide Mr.
B with the names and contact information regarding such individuals.

2. Matrimonial property

a) What is the value of Mr. B's corporate interests?

[
44
]

Mr. B is a shareholder in a group of six
companies, although it is only BI Corp. and a second company I shall call "905
Ltd." that remain active and have any value. In support of the valuation
of Mr. B's corporate interests, Ms. B called as an expert witness Mr. Lorne D.
Siebert, a Chartered Professional Accountant, Chartered Business Valuator and
Fellow of the Canadian Institute of Chartered Business Valuators. I accepted
his qualifications both as an expert and I accepted his evidence including his
conclusions. In fact, Mr. Siebert's conclusions were not seriously challenged
on cross-examination. The main points of contention related to the input value
for BI Corp.'s properties (the "BI Properties") and concerns related
to alleged double-counting of Mr. B's shareholder loans as capital and income. Mr.
B also pointed out that the valuation of his corporate interests did not account
for his personal tax liability. I will address each of these concerns.

[
45
]

Mr. Siebert assessed the fair market value of BI
Corp. and 905 Ltd. as going concerns on an asset-based approach in June 2017;
he then updated his report prior to trial in October 2018. Since the corporate
entities carry on real estate and investment activities, the share values
consist mostly of the market values of the respective assets, net of
liabilities. Mr. Siebert explained that he started by examining the corporate
balance sheets, and then he adjusted the book value to market value. In April
2017, the parties hired a licensed real estate appraiser to conduct an independent
appraisal of the BI Properties. The appraiser opined that their market value
was $4.75 million. Mr. Siebert used this appraisal figure in his first report.

[
46
]

Mr. B rejected Mr. Siebert's use of this $4.75 million figure as being inappropriate
for valuation at trial. He argues that he, Mr. S, and the corporate accountants
estimate that $4.3 million is a more appropriate current value for the BI
Properties. Despite this disagreement, Mr. B conceded in argument that he does
not otherwise take issue with Mr. Siebert's valuation methods; his primary
concern was the use of the $4.75 million input value. He argued as follows in
his written brief:

The Seibert Expert Report puts the estimated gross pre-tax
value at a range of $3,294,000 to $3,866,000 using a value of the 17
th

Ave property at $4.75 million, contrasted to the net after tax value calculated
by the corporate accountants of $2,251,282 at a value of $4.3 million.
Mr.
Seibert's gross pre-tax value is virtually identical to the net after tax value
once tax is actually taken into account for the BI Properties and adjusted from
a commercial value of $4.75 million to $4.3 million put forward in the
settlement offer.
[Emphasis added.]

Thus, aside from the disputed input
value, the parties do not disagree on the valuation process itself.

[
47
]

The parties also have somewhat different
approaches in addressing the eventual tax liabilities. Mr. B's reference to the
"net after tax value … for the BI Properties" deducts his own
personal income tax liability on the sale of his shares from the value of the
corporate entity. I find it is inappropriate, in the valuation of a business
entity, to consider the personal tax liability of the shareholder. Mr. Siebert
was asked to value the corporate entities. Whether or not Mr. B will be liable
for personal tax on the sale of his shares or on a distribution therefrom does
not affect the value of the corporations

report specifically states at paragraph 5.9 that the conclusions on fair market

Mr. B's investment in the Companies to be sold." Mr. Siebert reiterated
this point in cross-examination, namely, that the tax liability to the person
selling the shares is not part of the fair market value calculation for the
value of the business.

[
48

Nonetheless, I accept that Mr. B's personal tax liability is a relevant
consideration in the ultimate distribution of matrimonial property between the
parties. Just as the liability of a mortgage is deducted from the value of a matrimonial
home, the tax liability on Mr. B's share distribution should be deducted from the
value of the corporate entities for the purposes of the matrimonial property
distribution, since Mr. B is required to share only the net value of the asset as
matrimonial property. This is conceptually distinct, however, from considering
the personal tax liability as part of the business valuation
of the corporate entity.

[
49
]

Mr. B also argues that Mr. Siebert's inclusion
of Mr. B's shareholder loans as an asset belonging to the corporate entities
and as income for the purposes of calculating his Guideline income results in
double-dipping or double-accounting. He submits it is wrong to make him responsible
for higher child support resulting from a higher income occasioned by extensive
shareholder loans; and, at the same time, to require division of those same funds
as corporate assets in the matrimonial property distribution. He submits the
shareholder loans should be treated as either capital, or income, not both.

[
50
]

While at first blush this submission appears to
have merit, it fails to account for the true nature of the shareholder loans. It
is common practice to advance loans to shareholders and then use salary or
dividend declarations to clear the shareholder loan account. In the normal
course, the shareholder then declares the salary or dividends as taxable
income. If a loan from a corporation to a shareholder is not repaid directly or
through salary or dividends within one year, then the amount of the shareholder
loan is a deemed taxable benefit to the shareholder.

[
51
]

For so long as these shareholder loans remain
unpaid, they are reflected in the corporate accounting as assets to the
corporate entity because, in theory at least, the corporation can demand
repayment. In this case, the corporate records show that Mr. B owed money to
the corporate entities for most years relevant to this trial. The loans to Mr.
B are an asset to the corporate entities, which is why they are included in the
corporate valuation. Mr. B argues that by including these amounts as an asset
to the corporate entities, they are being double-counted both as income and as
a matrimonial property asset.

[
52
]

But the simple inclusion of the shareholder
loans as a corporate asset in the business valuation is not the end of the
analysis. When dividing up the total value of the corporations as between the
two equal shareholders (Mr. S and Mr. B), Mr. B's ultimate payout will be reduced
by the amount of his shareholder loans. The following example with simplified
numbers will help illustrate. If the corporate entities had a value of
$1,000,000, including $100,000 in shareholder loans owing back to the
corporation from Mr. B, then each 50% shareholder would be entitled to $500,000
of the total value. Yet Mr. B's distribution from the corporation would be only
$400,000, because he already took $100,000 of value in the form of a shareholder
loan. In essence, his $500,000 asset comprises $100,000 of debt forgiveness and
a $400,000 distribution.

[
53
]

There is no double-dipping because the value of
Mr. B's remaining property interest is reduced by the amount he has pre-taken
and the amount he pre-took was included in his income and forms the basis of
his Guideline income calculation. In this sample scenario, Mr. B would have a
$400,000 matrimonial asset to share with Ms. B, subject to any personal tax
liability.

54

approach. He states at paragraphs 1.4 & 5.8 of his valuation report that his
"valuation calculations include the value of shares owned by Mr. B less
the amount of shareholder loans owed by Mr. B to the various entities." He
repeats this statement in his updated valuation report.

b) Has each party established the validity of the loans

Both Mr. B and Ms. B allege that their mothers

,

2015 ABQB 50
at para
59 & 63
set out and applied a list of factors that are
useful for determining whether or not a loan exists between family members. In
that decision, Verville J. held that in order for the Court to conclude that
money as advanced between family members should be treated as a loan rather
than a gift, the Court must undertake a case-by-case analysis of the situation,
considering some of the following commonly arising factors:

•

Whether there were any contemporaneous documents
evidencing a loan;

•

Whether the manner for repayment is specified;

•

Whether there is security held for the loan;

•

Whether there are advances to one child and not
others, or advances of unequal amounts to various children;

•

Whether there was any demand for payment before
the separation of the parties;

•

Whether there has been any partial repayment;
and,

•

Whether there was any expectation, or
likelihood, of repayment.

purchased with the loaned funds. Mr. B has conceded that the full amount
remains owing to Ms. F. I find the evidence establishes that the funds advanced
by Ms. F to Mr. and Ms. B constitute a loan that is a joint matrimonial debt.

[

Ms. B also claims significant loans from her
mother to cover her post-separation expenses, some of which are documented in
signed loan agreements in the amounts of $9,000, $10,000, and $25,000. Ms. B
testified that her mother has been paying many of her credit card expenses

B's real estate practice.

66

While Ms. B's documentation satisfies me that
the advances from her mother were loans, rather than gifts, I do not accept
them as joint matrimonial debts. Ms. B borrowed these funds from her mother to
cover expenses in part because Mr. B was not providing adequate support. When
the support arrears are rectified, Ms. B can repay her mother whatever she
owes. If Ms. B spent more than she can repay, she will have to find some other
way to access funds. In short, I find that these post-separation loans are her

executed in 2006. Finally, Mr. B points to a caveat, which was executed

not established that the funds were intended as a loan at the time of the transfer.

not a joint matrimonial debt.

4. Spousal support

a) Is Ms. B entitled to spousal support?

[
170
]

Ms. B seeks spousal support on compensatory and
non-compensatory grounds. The
Divorce Act
requires me to consider the
conditions, means, needs and circumstances of the parties, including the length
of the time they cohabited, the functions performed by each spouse during the
marriage, and any order, agreement or arrangement related to support.

[
171
]

If upon considering these factors, entitlement
to spousal support is established, then the objectives of spousal support are
to recognize any economic advantages or disadvantages arising from the marriage
or its breakdown, apportion between the spouses any financial consequences
arising from the care of any children of the marriage, relieve any economic
hardship arising from the breakdown of the marriage, and in so far as
practicable, promote the self-sufficiency of each spouse within a reasonable
amount of time.

[
172
]

Spousal
support can have compensatory and non-compensatory elements. The purpose of
compensatory spousal support is to redress economic disadvantages arising from
the assumption of childcare or household responsibilities that resulted in the conferral
of economic advantages to the other spouse. The fact that a spouse was employed
outside the marriage or engaged in the same career throughout the marriage and
at its end does not necessarily preclude entitlement to spousal support on
compensatory grounds:
Chutter v Chutter
,
2008 BCCA 507
at para

71
.

[
173
]

Non-compensatory support is premised on the
interdependency arising from marital union and aims to narrow the gap between
the needs and means of the spouses upon marriage breakdown. The concept of "need"
goes beyond basic necessities and is specific to the circumstances of the
parties and the family as a whole. The longer the cohabitation and marriage,
the greater the presumption that each party is entitled to continue to live a
lifestyle approximating what they shared as a couple, assuming there are the
means to do so.

[
174
]

Ms. B claims entitlement to spousal support on
compensatory and non-compensatory grounds. She was 42 years old at the time of
separation, following a total of 19 years of cohabitation, including 14 years
of marriage. She was the primary caregiver for the children during the marriage
and since separation. She managed the children's activities and schedules and
tended to the household, including cleaning, laundry, grocery shopping, etc.
While Ms. B worked as a commercial real estate agent throughout the marriage in
some capacity, she could not dedicate herself full-time to this work.
Furthermore, her work was always secondary to the needs of the family.

[
175
]

Conversely, Mr. B worked without primary
responsibility for the household or children and received the benefit of being
able to develop his corporate interests into successful ventures. Ms. B
testified that they enjoyed a good lifestyle throughout the marriage and lived
without a budget. They lived in a beautiful home in Calgary, which they
renovated further, as well as a home in Arizona. They vacationed regularly in
British Columbia, Florida and Mexico. They drove luxury vehicles.

[
176
]

Mr. B has continued to spend liberally since
separation. There is evidence of two further luxury car purchases, monthly
payments to his girlfriend (from whom he is now separated), and significant
deposits into his bank accounts, which now appear to be depleted. He continued
to spend, all the while not meeting his full child support obligations.

[
177
]

Ms. B, by contrast, has experienced a
significant decrease in her household income. Her income in the three years
after the separation was between $22,000 and $35,000. It is only now that she
expects her income to climb into the $60,000 range. Ms. B has borrowed
extensively from her mother to meet her own and the children's needs.

[
178
]

I find that Ms. B has established a compensatory
and non-compensatory entitlement to spousal support. Ms. B was unable to fully
develop her career as a result of her parenting and household responsibilities.
Now she is unable to enjoy the parties’ previous lifestyle, to which she is
entitled after 19 years of cohabitation, without support. This said, I note
that neither party will be able to live in the manner to which they had become
accustomed, if for no other reason than two households cost more than one.
Also, Mr. B's work with Mr. S has ended, and only time will reveal what other
employment he will find in its place.

[
179
]

Ms. B has established entitlement to spousal
support. The remaining issues are the proper amount and duration.

$23,765. I note that this includes $8,200 in legal fees, which one would hope

guidance in the

calculations, which
provide ranges for support and duration.

Ms. B's counsel presented Divorcemate printouts
suggesting a total retroactive spousal support claim of $291,892. I find I cannot
rely on these figures. I have no way of ascertaining whether the Guideline
income figures were properly entered to reflect Mr. B's varied sources of
income, as detailed in Mr. Siebert's report. The
Spousal Support Advisory
Guidelines
explain at page 75 that the differing manner in which income tax
is treated, requires more detailed after-tax calculations, so as to more
accurately assess ability to pay. Since the
with child support
formula
of the SSAG uses the net incomes of the spouses, it is vital that the income
information be entered correctly; it is incorrect to simply input an adjusted
gross income figure into the employment income line, since the different tax
treatment of different types of income will lead to different net disposable
incomes in each household.

[
185
]

Furthermore, I have no way of knowing if the
section 7 expenses, which can significantly affect spousal support calculations,
were entered properly, particularly since I have not accepted all of Ms. B's

calculations, the 2016 tax rules to the 2016 SSAG calculations and so forth.

•

•

The SSAG ranges for 2018 fall between $5,089 and $6,938 per
month.
